🎙 Iran to deliver additional points on US counter-proposal: Foreign Ministry

📌 Tehran, IRNA — Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei says Iran will convey its additional points on a US counter-proposal to an earlier Iranian plan for ending the war after conducting the necessary assessments.

Baqaei made the remarks during his weekly press briefing in Tehran on Sunday, in response to a question about Iran’s response to Washington’s counter-proposal to Tehran’s seven-day plan for opening the Strait of Hormuz.
​
The seven-day plan was conveyed to the US through Qatari mediators two weeks ago, while an Iranian delegation headed by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi was in New York for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly. Washington delivered its response and counter-proposal a week later, while the Iranian delegation was in Doha on its way back home from New York. The Iranian government confirmed last Wednesday that it had received the US response.
​
“Our positions were conveyed to the mediator during the brief stop we made in Doha on our way back. The proposals put forward by the Americans are more or less in line with their previous positions and specifically concern nuclear issues. We made it clear that, at this stage, our focus is on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz,” the spokesperson said.
​
Restoring security to the Strait of Hormuz requires the US to take specific steps, including ending disruptions to Iran’s commercial shipping and interventionist measures and sanctions, including those imposed after the June 18 memorandum of understanding, he noted.
​
“The considerations raised by the Americans and conveyed to us by the Qatari mediator were discussed at that meeting, and our considerations were also addressed in return. We will conduct the necessary reviews regarding some of the details and will convey our additional points to the other side as well,” Baqaei said.
​
He reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz was secure before the US and Israel launched their war of aggression on Iran on February 28. Baqaei stressed that Iran uses every opportunity for diplomacy to prevent an escalation of tensions and restore peace, even if that opportunity is grim.
​
“The reality is that previous experience and the US stance show that the other side is not serious in using diplomacy,” he said.
​
The spokesperson meanwhile rejected news reports claiming that Iran, in its seven-day plan, had proposed sanctions relief in return for the resumption of inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency at Iranian nuclear sites.
​
“We did not, in principle, enter into discussions on the nuclear issue in exchange for sanctions relief. Our task was to communicate our conditions, which we conveyed to the mediators in the form of a proposal that came to be known as the “seven-day plan,” he explained.
​
Baqaei also dismissed US President Donald Trump’s claim that he does not know who is negotiating on behalf of Iran. The spokesperson called the claim baseless, saying that no country has the same level of cohesion and order in decision-making as Iran.
​
“The Americans know very well how decisions are made in the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Baqaei said, adding that the problem instead lies in the US, where different parties undermine each other’s roles and contradictory approaches are a major issue.

* The Fictional "Secret Meeting": There was no secret meeting to plot a fake hijacking. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did travel to the UAE, but investigative reporting by outlets like Haaretz confirmed the meeting was a political push regarding regional tensions with Iran and managing political damage over leaks ahead of the upcoming election. The idea that a prime minister would fly to a foreign nation to coordinate the stabbing of an Indian pilot by an Omani national on a commercial aircraft is a total fairytale.

* The Nosedive Myth: The plane did not go into a vertical, structural "nosedive" that would rip the wings off. It was a chaotic, high-speed altitude drop during a manual struggle over the flight sticks, which the aircraft's aerodynamic limits are built to withstand.

* The "Plummeting Tin Can" Physics Failure: The passengers weren't casually strolling. The aircraft did experience a sudden, terrifying altitude drop when the attacker grabbed the controls, plunging thousands of feet in less than a minute. However, an emergency descent creates high G-forces and immense chaos, not zero gravity. Passengers (including an off-duty plumber and dentist) frantically lunged forward, crawled, and pushed their way through the released door to put the attacker in a chokehold.

* The Election Context: While Israel's Knesset elections are indeed taking place on October 27 and the political climate is highly volatile, using a real political date to claim a mid-air terrorist attack over Saudi Arabia was a staged performance is a classic logical fallacy.

* The Tracking Codes: The plane never 'vanished' from tracking. Radar data explicitly logged the cockpit transponder switching from emergency code 7700 to hijack code 7500 during the struggle. That's why Saudi air traffic control immediately cleared the plane to drop altitude and land at the nearest runway in Tabuk.

THE WATER CUP

* The Sealed Cup Self-Own: Flydubai, Emirates, and most international airlines serve individual water in pre-packaged, heat-sealed plastic tubs. The cup literally has a clear plastic lid on it. It couldn't spill or splash during a descent even if it wanted to because it’s airtight.

* The Fluid Mechanics Fail: Even if it were open, the passenger video was filmed after the backup pilots regained control, leveled the plane, and stabilised the flight path. Liquid doesn't stay permanently sloshing and swirling in a cup forever just because a vehicle dropped altitude minutes prior. Gravity settles it back down the millisecond the forces equalise.

THE COCKPIT DOOR OPENING DIRECTION 

The Physics of Flight: Cockpit Doors Open INWARD

On the Boeing 737 (including the MAX 8 involved in the Flydubai incident), the reinforced security flight deck door is mechanically hinged to open inward, swinging forward into the cockpit itself, not backward into the passenger cabin.

Why They Are Engineered That Way: If the main passenger cabin experiences a sudden drop in air pressure (depressurisation), the massive pressure differential will push the cockpit door forward. Because it opens inward, it can swing forward onto its decompression panels to instantly equalise the air pressure between both compartments, protecting the plane's structural integrity. If it opened into the cabin, it would get jammed shut by the pressure.

Forced Entry Protection: It makes it significantly harder for an attacker in the passenger cabin to force their way in. Pushing against a door that slams shut into a solid, reinforced metal frame is much more secure than a door that could be pulled open or kicked down into the aisle.

The Physical Block Explained: Because the door physically swings forward into the cockpit, the wounded captain (who was sitting or lying on the flight deck floor right next to the pedestal console) was physically occupying the exact space the door needed to swing into.
